stories.title: What it takes to build a sustainable data centre for the AI era
stories.summary: From factory-built modules to on-site water treatment, Bridge Data Centres is building sustainability into every stage of a data centre’s life

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
From factory-built modules to on-site water treatment, Bridge Data Centres is building sustainability into every stage of a data centre’s life

AS ARTIFICIAL intelligence and cloud computing reshape how economies grow, data centres have become essential infrastructure. They enable economies to connect, businesses to innovate and communities to take part in a more digital future.

For Bridge Data Centres (BDC), this means building data centres to provide the digital infrastructure that supports growth across Asia-Pacific and beyond. Chief executive officer Eric Fan says the company aims to meet rising demand while helping define what responsible digital infrastructure should become.

That makes sustainability a core part of BDC’s growth strategy, he adds. Sustainability shapes every stage of a data centre’s life, from site selection and design to construction, energy and water sourcing, and daily operations.

The company’s latest Sustainability Report shows what this looks like in practice. For instance, at BDC’s MY06 campus in Johor, Malaysia, a large part of the data centre was built off-site before it reached the site.

BDC utilised Prefabricated Prefinished Volumetric Construction (PPVC), where data centre modules were made and tested in factories, then installed on the campus. MY06 was completed 40 per cent faster than with traditional methods, with less waste and noise produced on site. BDC was the first data centre developer in South-east Asia to adopt PPVC.

When the campus was running, BDC’s operations team lowered fan speeds and raised the temperature set point by one degree on air-conditioning units in an electrical equipment room. Energy used to cool that room fell by nearly a quarter. MY06 now runs at an annualised Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE\*) below 1.2.

The MY06 campus also made BDC the first data centre operator to receive the BCA Green Mark Platinum award for a facility outside Singapore. BDC has since signed a Memorandum of Understanding with BCA International to support the adoption of Singapore’s Green Mark standards in global data centre developments.

AI adds pressure. Each rack holds more computing power and produces more heat. BDC designs cooling – from air to liquid cooling – to suit each site’s climate and water supply.

BDC has put numbers against these ambitions. Its near-term emissions targets, validated by the Science Based Targets initiative, call for it to cut absolute Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions by 42 per cent by 2030, from a 2024 base year. It is also committed to 100 per cent renewable electricity by 2040 under RE100.

These targets, along with projects such as MY06, are set out in BDC’s 2025 Sustainability Report, which is prepared with reference to the GRI Standards and IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures.

Fan says the next generation of data centres “must deliver scale and reliability, but they must also be more efficient in energy use, more thoughtful in water management, more resilient to climate and operational risks”.

## Renewable energy and water treatment for greener data centres

Several of BDC’s projects focus on the two areas Fan highlights: energy and water.

In Malaysia, BDC was the first data centre operator to sign a 400 MW agreement with the national utility under the Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme. The agreement is for its MY07 campus in Johor, Malaysia.

BDC completed its inaugural hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO)-powered backup fuel pilot in Asia-Pacific at one of the company’s data centre campuses. The pilot demonstrated that HVO can be used as a cleaner alternative to conventional diesel for critical data centre backup power systems. Produced from waste-based feedstock, HVO requires no equipment changes and can cut greenhouse-gas emissions by up to 90 per cent.

At MY07, BDC built Malaysia’s first water treatment plant within a data centre site. Using membrane bioreactor and reverse osmosis technologies, the plant treats effluent into high-grade water for cooling. Running since 2025, it reduces the campus’s reliance on potable water by up to 40 per cent.

BDC has also endorsed the UN Global Compact’s CEO Water Mandate.

## Training and talent development in data centre operations

Data centres depend on specialised skills. BDC brings together an international team with expertise in engineering, critical operations, safety management and customer delivery.

The company invests in building those skills. Training reaches every BDC employee, from leadership development and technical certifications to education sponsorships for staff pursuing degrees. Total training hours more than doubled year-on-year.

In Malaysia, BDC works with institutes of higher learning to grow local talent. Its Management Trainee Programme prepares engineering graduates for roles in critical operations.

Diversity is part of that strength. Women hold a third of C-suite leadership roles and close to a third of senior management positions. BDC is a signatory to the Women’s Empowerment Principles, established by UN Women and the UN Global Compact, and sees diverse leadership as a driver of balanced decision-making.

“BDC will continue to build with purpose and discipline,” says Fan. “We will invest in technologies that improve reliability and efficiency, strengthen our climate and resource management, enhance transparency and work with partners to scale practical solutions.”

Find out more about BDC’s sustainability efforts in its 2025 Sustainability Report.

*\*PUE measures how much total power a facility uses for each unit that reaches its IT equipment. The closer to 1.0, the more energy efficient. PUE is the standard industry metric used to measure data centre energy efficiency, defined by ISO 30134-2.*

stories.title: Johor data centres could consume over 90% of peninsula's additional power generation by 2031 — BMI
stories.summary: Johor's booming data centre industry could consume more than 90% of the additional electricity generated in Peninsular Malaysia in the next five years, raising concerns over power supply and grid infrastructure constraints, according to a report by BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 23): Johor's booming data centre industry could consume more than 90% of the additional electricity generated in Peninsular Malaysia in the next five years, raising concerns over power supply and grid infrastructure constraints, according to a report by BMI, a Fitch Solutions company.

BMI estimated that Johor’s data centres would require about 30 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity annually by 2031, accounting for 18% of Peninsular Malaysia’s total electricity supply, up from 6% in 2026.

BMI warned that Johor could face the tightest electricity supply constraints among the data centre hubs it researched in the region, including Sydney and Melbourne in Australia, and Batam in Indonesia.

Johor currently has about 825 megawatts (MW) of operational data centre capacity, with another 3.9 gigawatts (GW) expected to be added over the next three to five years, due to growing demand for cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI).

Major projects include YTL Power International Bhd’s (KL:YTLPOWR) 1.2GW data centre campus, which is expected to have its first 300MW operational by the first quarter of 2027, and a 300MW facility in Sedenak owned by Vantage Data Centers — backed by US alternative asset manager DigitalBridge Group Inc.

BMI expects some planned data centres to face delays, particularly those that have yet to secure electricity connections, even as demand for AI computing continues to grow.

It said the bigger challenge lies in connecting new data centres to the electricity grid, rather than generating enough power.

“Grid infrastructure takes considerably longer to develop than data centres, meaning headline generation capacity can overstate how much power is actually accessible to new projects,” said the macroeconomics research firm.

Although Peninsular Malaysia's grid is operating at an estimated 30% of its overall capacity, data centre developments are concentrated in areas such as Sedenak and Nusajaya, where local electricity infrastructure is becoming strained.

BMI noted that Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) plans to invest RM43 billion in grid upgrades, but major infrastructure projects typically take five to 10 years to complete, potentially delaying new data centre developments.

The research unit also expects Malaysia to increase its gas-fired electricity generation to meet growing demand, with some scheduled power plant closures potentially postponed to ensure sufficient supply.

While electricity generation is expected to meet demand under BMI's base-case projections, higher-than-expected data centre activity could strain supply.

stories.title: Europe's digital infrastructure faces power, connectivity challenges
stories.summary: Europe's AI sector faces a new challenge in delivering power, connectivity, and capacity for development, despite abundant demand. Data centre construction is often the easiest part, with external dependencies posing significant hurdles.
stories.content:
Delivering adequate power, connectivity, and capacity to support Europe’s growing artificial intelligence (AI) sector remains a key challenge, despite high demand, according to panellists at Capacity Europe 2026.Paula Cogan, managing director, EMEA at Digital Realty, stated that building a facility is often the easiest part of the process. She noted that the primary challenge lies in external dependencies, including power availability, grid connections, permitting, and increasing public scrutiny.AI workloads are driving rapid demand for capacity, making access to electricity the industry’s main constraint. Brenden Rawle of Equinix highlighted the uncertainty surrounding utility connection timelines, which impacts effective planning for large-scale deployments.AI training workloads are increasingly drawn to regions such as the Nordics, which offer access to large blocks of affordable power. Cogan also observed a convergence, with customers seeking to run both AI use cases and cloud deployments on the same platform.
### Collaboration and Connectivity

Connectivity is becoming increasingly important in digital infrastructure planning. Cogan emphasised that a data centre requires a deep connectivity ecosystem to function effectively.Joe Scattareggia, executive vice president at Colt Technology Services, stressed the value of involving connectivity providers early in data centre development. He stated that early involvement simplifies integration into global network planning, budgets, and forecasts.Rawle confirmed that Equinix collaborated with connectivity partners years before opening a major London development. Panellists collectively argued that no single organisation can resolve Europe’s infrastructure challenges alone, making collaboration vital.Scattareggia urged early and open collaboration, acknowledging the competitive nature of sites but highlighting the necessity of trust. Cogan echoed this, advocating for greater transparency on demand forecasts and infrastructure needs across the ecosystem, including grid providers and communities.Despite challenges related to energy use and sustainability, demand for digital infrastructure and investment levels continue to rise. Scattareggia concluded that the sector is experiencing a unique opportunity with unprecedented investment.

- Cloud, Colocation & Connectivity
- 2 min Read

stories.title: Nebius Group secures multi billion loan to fund AI infrastructure expansion
stories.summary: Nebius Group (Nebius), an AI cloud company, has entered into a US$ 3.5 billion senior secured credit facility provided by Citi, an American multinational investment bank and financial services corporation, to help finance its data center expansion and GPU procurement to increase its global infrastructure capacity. According to a press release, the 364 day facility […]
stories.content:
Nebius Group (Nebius), an AI cloud company, has entered into a US$ 3.5 billion senior secured credit facility provided by Citi, an American multinational investment bank and financial services corporation, to help finance its data center expansion and GPU procurement to increase its global infrastructure capacity.

According to a press release, the 364 day facility carries an initial interest rate of Term SOFR plus 2.75 percent per year, rising to a maximum of 3.5 percent, subject to other adjustments. The proceeds will also be available for general corporate purposes.

The loan forms part of Nebius’s broader funding strategy, which combines customer prepayments and operating cash flow with external financing. By securing capital through different sources and at different stages of its expansion, the company aims to manage its borrowing costs while retaining flexibility over when and how it raises additional funds.

“We continue to execute our funding strategy as planned, and are pleased to have secured this financing from a leading global financial institution,” said Ophir Nave, Chief Operating Officer, Nebius. “This facility provides additional financing to support our near-term capacity build-out. We still have a range of capital sources available to us to finance the next phase of growth, including asset-backed financing based on investment-grade customer commitments of more than US$ 40 billion of long-term contracts.”

The Citi facility would support the company’s near-term infrastructure investments while leaving other financing options available for future growth. Citi acted as mandated lead arranger, agent and security agent for the facility and Nebius also pointed to asset backed financing as a potential source of funding.

stories.title: SK Group’s data centre arm in talks to fund US$350 billion AI buildout
stories.summary: This involves a plan to develop 15GW of capacity in South Korea by 2030

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic
The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
This involves a plan to develop 15GW of capacity in South Korea by 2030

SK HYPER is in talks with big tech firms and financial investors to secure funding for an envisioned US$350 billion data centre buildout, joining a global rush to roll out artificial intelligence infrastructure despite concerns about future demand.

The SK Group’s fledgling data centre arm has begun discussions with potential partners to help finance a plan to build 15 gigawatts (GW) of data centre capacity in South Korea by 2035, said Chung Suk-geun, SK Hyper’s chief executive officer.

The first 5 GW phase alone would require US$350 billion including equipment, he told Bloomberg Television.

The company aims to secure its first round of external capital by the end of 2026 or early 2027, followed by further fundraising over the next three to four years. SK plans to share the overall cost with data centre tenants and outside investors, he added.

“We are under discussions with many strategic and financial partners,” Chung said in an interview. “We want to be prepared for meeting the market demand by making data centres in Korea.”

SK is pursuing an ambitious blueprint at a time markets are gyrating on fears of an AI bubble. Investors funding data centre projects are getting nervous that spending on future AI services will not be enough to justify the trillions of dollars flowing into a global computing buildout.

Chung said his company would adjust the pace of investment according to actual demand, rather than commit to the entire plan upfront. “We are going to manage our risk appropriately, meeting with market demand,” he added.

Established in July as a unit of SK Telecom, SK Hyper is seeking to attract global technology companies to South Korea as a base for AI training and operations, serving Asian markets such as Japan and Taiwan rather than relying solely on domestic demand.

SK Group has plenty of affiliates – with expertise in chips, energy and telecommunications – that should help offset relatively high electricity costs by improving computing efficiency, Chung said. SK Telecom itself plans to invest 750 billion won (US$567 million) in SK Hyper by 2030.

SK Hyper is developing a 900 megawatt (MW) project in the southern industrial city of Ulsan, alongside a previously announced 100 MW project for Amazon Web Services. It is in talks with the government to secure additional sites, Chung said.

It is also exploring opportunities to serve governments in Asia and the Middle East, offering computing capacity and AI models as an integrated package. Chung said SK Hyper could begin generating revenue as early as 2027, ahead of the planned completion of its initial data centres in 2029. BLOOMBERG

stories.title: AI data centre backlash threatens Australia’s US$70 bil dream
stories.summary: More than three-quarters of data centres set to be built around Australia’s biggest cities are at risk from stretched power grids and local opposition, threatening the country’s ambition to become an artificial intelligence (AI) hub for the Asia Pacific region.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
(Oct 23): More than three-quarters of data centres set to be built around Australia’s biggest cities are at risk from stretched power grids and local opposition, threatening the country’s ambition to become an artificial intelligence (AI) hub for the Asia Pacific region.

Of the 40-plus large centres planned or under construction in Sydney and Melbourne — representing more than A$100 billion (US$70 billion or RM286 billion) of projected investment — just 23% have confirmed publicly that they have secured electricity supply or grid connections, according to a *Bloomberg* review of company disclosure. Those agreements, a gauge of whether or not a project is advancing, suggest significant setbacks and potential delays.

Australia has bet heavily on a data-centre boom that is intended to capitalise on its vast open spaces as well as clean-energy potential. To date, though, most of the project pipeline is clustered around Sydney and Melbourne — where almost two in five of its inhabitants live — in order to harness existing fiber networks and reliable power. Those operations put more strain on already stretched infrastructure, and leave developers on a collision course with residents.

In Sydney, seven of 28 active projects have confirmed power, according to *Bloomberg*’s analysis. In Melbourne, the figure drops to three out of 15.

*Bloomberg* contacted 25 developers to verify public disclosure on power supply and the status of more than 40 projects. Operator GreenSquare declined to comment on its power arrangements but said it was “working closely with relevant authorities and infrastructure partners to support long-term operational performance”. CDC Data Centres said it had “robust delivery plans in place for all sites currently under construction” with power delivery timelines as anticipated.

Nine others declined to comment or didn’t directly answer queries on future projects. The rest did not respond.

The consequences of friction and delays are already apparent. Operator Nextdc Ltd slashed its profit forecast this week after Melbourne residents blocked the installation of towering transmission lines, almost halving the value of its shares.

In Sydney, Goodman Group abandoned its A$1.2 billion Project Mars development last month. The proposed 90-megawatt facility would have been built about 20 metres from the nearest home and 160 metres from a public school, prompting hundreds of objections to be submitted during the planning process.

“The social licence for Australian data centres is becoming an increasingly significant headwind,” Morgans Financial Ltd analyst Nick Harris wrote this week. “Investors are becoming concerned more delays could occur and question what the knock-on effect might be.”

The gulf between announced projects and those that will be built is also beginning to emerge in official data. Over a third of proposed data centres that would tap Australia’s main grid were cancelled last year, according to the Australian Energy Market Operator.

Part of the issue is the sheer scale of the build out. The country has more than 20 gigawatts of capacity in announced and early-stage data centre projects compared to an operational fleet of just 1.5 gigawatts, according to *BloombergNEF.*

“Access to energy is already a major issue,” said *BNEF* analyst Tushna Mehta. “Data centre capacity is being built much faster than the new generation needed to supply it.”

These hurdles are raising questions about the government’s push to make Australia a hub for the wider region, courting investors and seeking to streamline approvals even as practical constraints remain. Land may be plentiful, but data centres need access to high-voltage electricity lines and other infrastructure. Building further from the major cities can have advantages, but also means hefty investment in new transmission lines and telecommunications.

Sydney’s electricity grid is already struggling to accommodate the scale of the boom. Transgrid, which operates the statewide power network, said in August the city doesn’t have enough transmission capacity to connect any of the 20 gigawatts of inquiries it’s received from large new power users.

Half of that proposed demand has emerged within a 12km radius of its Sydney West substation, Transgrid said — equivalent to the peak winter electricity load of the entire state of New South Wales, in one small area.

That strain is expected to intensify, and quickly. Australia already has more than 160 operating data centres, concentrated mainly in Sydney and Melbourne, which consume about 2% of electricity supplied by the country’s grids. AEMO has projected this could rise by a quarter each year to roughly 6% by 2030, and 13% by 2036.

Another hurdle is access to water. Industry-commissioned analysis estimates Australian data centres use about 5.5 gigalitres of water each year, largely for cooling — equivalent to roughly 0.04% of national consumption. But the local impact could be far greater when projects are clustered together, including in growth corridors already facing stress from drought.

Residents living near Nextdc’s facility in Melbourne’s West Footscray — about 15 metres from it, in some cases — told a parliamentary inquiry last month they wanted compensation for noise, pollution and potential fire risks.

“What we are seeing is rising public resistance to AI, particularly generative AI,” said Bronwyn Cumbo, who researches data centres at the University of Technology Sydney. “Many are planned to be built near homes, schools, farmland and natural areas, and alter the experience and livability of these places.”

stories.title: Reconfigured UPS systems can stabilise data center power fluctuations
stories.summary: Data centers are exploring reconfigured uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems to enhance power stability and prevent fluctuations during grid disturbances. This approach aims to reduce stress on the broader power system and meet emerging ride-through requirements.
stories.content:
Data centers typically switch to emergency power during grid outages, which can cause instability across the broader power grid. A proposed solution involves reconfiguring UPS systems to support stability on both the grid-side and load-side.This reconfiguration uses a double conversion UPS with grid-side, load-side, and battery DC/DC converters, paired with a continuously running battery. The battery acts as a buffer, supplying or absorbing excess power to balance grid and data center demands.The grid-side converter helps smooth demand changes and supports grid stability, while the load-side converter ensures steady power to IT equipment. The system could also be modified for grid-support functions, managing voltage, reactive power, frequency response, and ride-through during faults.A test system with an AI data center training load profile of 100 MW peak demonstrated the UPS absorbing major load fluctuations. The test showed the reconfigured UPS maintained stable power during a 100-millisecond, three-phase-to-ground fault with no significant interruption on the load side.Regulators such as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) are considering broader reforms for large-load interconnections. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) is developing mandatory reliability standards for computational loads.Texas, through the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), is furthest along with specific requirements. ERCOT's framework applies to facilities of 75 MW or more and proposes rules requiring qualifying data centers to remain connected through defined disturbances rather than immediately dropping from the grid. Dr. Chandana Karawita, a senior technical manager at Ramboll, noted this practical, converter-based configuration offers a pathway to keep critical digital infrastructure online while reducing stress on the broader power system.

- Energy, Cooling & Sustainability

stories.title: Liquid cooling stretches AI data centre grid capacity
stories.summary: Liquid cooling can help Australian AI data centres maximise their use of capped grid connections. It reduces cooling overhead, freeing up power for IT equipment. This approach is crucial given the growing demand for high-density compute.
stories.content:
AI data centres in Australia are facing grid capacity constraints, particularly in New South Wales and Victoria, according to the Schneider Electric Blog. Cooling efficiency directly influences the amount of power available for IT equipment within a fixed grid connection.Lowering Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) can significantly increase theoretical IT capacity. For instance, a 100 MW connection with a PUE of 1.20 yields 83.3 MW of IT capacity, compared to 64.5 MW at a PUE of 1.55.Liquid cooling can reduce the power consumed by fans, air movement, and mechanical cooling, thereby freeing up capacity for compute loads. The potential gains depend on the specific architecture implemented across the thermal system.
### Cooling architectures and deployment

Rear-door heat exchangers (RDHx) capture hot exhaust air at the rack, transferring heat to liquid. This method can reduce room-cooling demand and support higher-density racks, especially in existing colocation halls.Direct-to-chip (DTC) cooling uses cold plates on high-power components like CPUs and GPUs. Heat Dissipation Units (HDUs) can transfer heat from the liquid loop into data-hall air where facility water is unavailable. This architecture allows direct-to-chip cooling without extending a facility-water loop to each deployment.Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) transfer heat from the technology cooling loop into the facility-water system, keeping the two loops hydraulically separated. This can reduce demand on fans and air handlers by allowing more heat to bypass room-air infrastructure.Cooling and electrical designs must be planned together. Reducing mechanical load creates usable IT headroom only when the electrical architecture can deliver that released capacity to the compute load. Hyperscalers, colocation operators, neocloud providers, and developers each have distinct cooling priorities and architectural needs.

- Energy, Cooling & Sustainability

stories.title: Nvidia CEO links neocloud demand to UK grid stall
stories.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stated that strong demand for AI compute capacity supports neocloud providers despite rising financing pressure. His comments followed Microsoft's withdrawal from Nscale's Essex data center project due to UK grid delays.
stories.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said demand for AI compute will support neocloud providers despite increasing financing pressure. Speaking to press at GTC Berlin, Huang noted that Nvidia had "invested enough" in neocloud providers. He described their capacity demand as "incredible," with operators "completely sold out."Huang argued that the need for capital stems from strong demand, not structural weakness. Nvidia's support includes guaranteeing utilisation floors for partners such as Sharon AI, agreeing to rent idle capacity if customer demand falls short.His remarks came days after Microsoft withdrew from its agreement to anchor Nscale's planned data center in Loughton, Essex. The site faces potential grid power delays until the early to mid-2030s. Loughton was initially announced in January 2025 as a 50MW site scheduled for Q4 2026 activation.Nscale told Reuters that its relationship with Microsoft remained strong and that the grid issue did not impact other contracts. Nscale affirmed its commitment to the Loughton project and is exploring alternative power sources. Huang acknowledged that faster manufacturing does not eliminate the need for more energy, describing AI's power demand as a significant opportunity for market-driven investment in sustainable energy.
### Infrastructure Challenges

The Loughton delay highlights the gap between AI demand and the necessary infrastructure. A recent Capacity roundtable in London revealed that 70 per cent of infrastructure leaders expect grid connections to exceed 18 months.Neoclouds typically have high capital costs, concentrated customer bases, and hardware plans tied to specific sites. This makes them more vulnerable to grid connection delays. For Nvidia, a delayed site can mean supply redirection. For a neocloud, a missed grid date can result in a lost customer.The Loughton setback follows an earlier pause in April for Nscale's UK Stargate project with OpenAI and Nvidia, which cited high energy costs. Nscale is pursuing alternative power for the Essex site, but on-site generation also faces lead times, with speakers at Capacity Europe noting generator lead times of up to two years.

stories.title: CBRE to acquire Onnec Group for up to £760 million
stories.summary: CBRE has agreed to acquire London-based Onnec Group, a data center infrastructure specialist, for up to £760 million. The deal will extend CBRE’s technical services across Europe and Asia-Pacific. This builds on previous acquisitions in the US market.
stories.content:
CBRE, a US property services group, has agreed to acquire London-based data center infrastructure specialist Onnec Group for up to £760 million.The acquisition will extend CBRE’s technical services business across Europe and Asia-Pacific. CBRE will pay £460 million upfront, with an additional £300 million potentially payable over several years if Onnec meets specified growth targets.The deal adds Onnec’s networking and connectivity expertise to CBRE’s existing data center facilities management capabilities. This allows CBRE to offer a broader range of infrastructure services across multiple regions.
### Global Infrastructure Strategy

CBRE has been expanding its technical capabilities through acquisitions in recent years. In 2024, the company acquired Direct Line Global, a US-based specialist in infrastructure design, installation, and maintenance for data center operators.This was followed in November 2025 by the $1.2 billion acquisition of Pearce Services. That deal expanded CBRE’s expertise across critical power and cooling, renewable energy infrastructure, and telecommunications networks.Onnec will extend this strategy across Europe and Asia-Pacific, complementing CBRE’s existing data center infrastructure services in the US. Vikram Kohli, Chief Operating Officer at CBRE, stated that the company is pursuing a strategy to build a global infrastructure services business.CBRE expects Onnec to generate approximately £370 million in revenue and more than £50 million in core EBITDA in 2027. The company forecasts its Critical Infrastructure Services business, which will include Onnec, to generate nearly $4.5 billion in revenue that year.Across its wider infrastructure services activities, CBRE expects revenue to reach nearly $7 billion in 2027.

stories.title: AI drives hybrid liquid cooling adoption in data centres
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence workloads are pushing data centre thermal management beyond air-only systems. Hybrid cooling architectures, combining air and direct liquid cooling, are becoming essential. This approach helps operators balance high-density demands with existing infrastructure.
stories.content:
AI workloads, which are significantly more power-dense and less predictable than traditional operations, require advanced thermal management. Liquid cooling has become essential for handling these AI and high-performance computing (HPC) demands.Air cooling remains viable up to 20 to 40 kilowatts (kW) per rack. However, GPU-accelerated AI racks commonly operate between 40 kW and over 100 kW, with next-generation systems projected to exceed 200 kW.Liquid cooling is up to 3,000 times more effective at transferring heat than air. This efficiency prevents thermal throttling and protects infrastructure return on investment (ROI). Most facilities are adopting hybrid cooling models, integrating traditional air architectures with direct-to-chip systems.
### Hybrid Cooling Dominance

Through 2027 and 2028, hybrid thermal strategies are expected to dominate transitions. Data centres must accommodate both legacy IT equipment and next-generation AI accelerators within the same facility. Brownfield retrofits in existing air-cooled facilities mean air cooling will remain crucial for ancillary systems and lower-density zones.Operators can deploy mixed architectures, such as direct-to-chip cold plates and Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) for dense AI clusters. They can manage residual heat with Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAHs) or fan-assisted Rear-Door Heat Exchangers (RDHx).
### Operational Challenges and Benefits

Navigating the operational complexity of a hybrid cooling environment presents a significant challenge. Cooling now requires the convergence of IT, mechanical engineering, and software management. Facilities must manage fluid chemistry, leak detection, risk mitigation, and sophisticated maintenance workflows.The industry also faces a talent gap, with Uptime Institute reporting that nearly two-thirds of operators struggle to hire and retain qualified staff. This shortage highlights the need for expertise across liquid cooling systems and integrated infrastructure. Addressing this will require new training models, deeper vendor collaboration, and greater reliance on managed services.While liquid infrastructure demands higher upfront capital expenditure (CapEx), it delivers better Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) over time. This improvement is due to enhanced efficiency and density. Advanced liquid cooling solutions can reduce total facility energy consumption by up to 40 per cent and cut water use by 20 to 90 per cent. It also unlocks opportunities for heat reuse, allowing operators to redirect waste heat to adjacent buildings or district heating systems.

stories.title: Microsoft files for data center campus in Floyd County, Georgia
stories.summary: Will feature three data center buildings
stories.content:
In a Development of Regional Impact application submitted on October 20, the company reveals it is seeking to build a three-building data center campus on 349 acres of land at 0 Huffaker Road in Rome. Microsoft acquired the property in 2023, at the time calling it "Project Firecracker."

Dubbed ATL80, all three buildings will total up to 1,659,000 sq ft (154,126 sqm) of floor space. Microsoft estimates the project will be valued at $360 million once built out and will provide $35m in annual local tax revenue.

The company estimates that the project will be completed by 2032 and will employ 150 people once operational.

Total power capacity will be 422MW and provided by Georgia Power, and Microsoft estimates that the maximum water supply required will be 13,500 gallons (51,103 liters) per day.

Rome is located Northwest of Atlanta, Georgia's main data center hub.

The filing comes just one month after Microsoft submitted a Developments of Regional Impact application with the Georgia Department of Community Affairs for ATL50, a two-building campus in Union City totaling 910,000 sq ft (84,540 sqm) on an 88-acre parcel west of Stonewall Tell Road and north of Koweta Road. The site is set to launch in 2032.

The company has a number of data center projects across Georgia, both operating and under development, including in Fairburn, Douglasville, Palmetto, Rome, East Point, Tyrone, and more. Atlanta is home to one of Microsoft's major "Fairwater" data centers, launching in November 2025.

Microsoft announced plans for a cloud region in 2021, revealing in December last year that the Fairwater site would be incorporated, as would developments in Fulton County, outside of Atlanta, having broken ground in July 2024, and two other projects on the outskirts of Atlanta; in East Point, Fulton County; and Douglasville, Douglas County.

stories.title: Arbol launches moratorium risk insurance coverage
stories.summary: First-of-its-kind cover will pay out on suspension of data center construction
stories.content:
Insurance provider Arbol has launched a product line covering data center moratorium risk.

The cover, which Arbol said is first-of-its-kind, pays out when a covered government action takes effect, resulting in the suspension of data center construction, and remains in force beyond a defined waiting period.

The company said this type of risk was previously considered “uninsurable.”

“As government action does not result in physical loss and falls outside the scope of standard insurance, developers have traditionally been left to lobby it, litigate it or absorb it. Arbol has made the exposure transferable by applying the specialist underwriting and alternative capital capabilities it uses across other classes that the market finds difficult to write,” the company added.

According to *DCD’s* analysis, there have been nearly 500 individual moratoriums proposed across the US since January, with 340 of these now authorized.

Public opposition to data center development has grown, with concerns over energy prices, water usage, and environmental impact causing the most concern.

Some moratoriums have been introduced specifically to curb the construction of in-progress projects.

One developer whose project was halted due to a moratorium has challenged the stay in court, arguing that a pause impacted the company’s property rights.

*DCD* analysis found that these issues have transcended being county- and city-level concerns and are now reaching the upper echelons of government. In the US, specifically, 80 percent of gubernatorial candidates have expressed a stance on data centers, with many discussing statewide moratoriums on their construction.

In July, New York became the first US state to impose a moratorium on new large-scale data centers.

stories.title: Canada's Uniserve to launch 1MW data center in Vancouver
stories.summary: Company developing facility next door to existing data center
stories.content:
Canadian IT solutions provider Uniserve Communications Corporation is developing a new data center in Vancouver adjacent to its existing facility. The firm has also secured a new customer set to host GPU hardware in its facilities.

Founded in 1988, Uniserve offers IT services, including data center solutions, colocation, cloud, and business Internet.

The company said this year that its data center expansion plans are part of a multi-year strategy to “evolve from a traditional service provider into a vertically integrated digital infrastructure platform purpose-built for Canadian businesses.”

Its existing VAN-1 site is located at 333 Terminal Avenue in Vancouver. Each floor of the eight-story multi-tenant office building spans 20,000 sq ft (1,858 sqm), though only a portion of the building is data center space.

The company first announced plans to expand its existing data center footprint in September 2025. At the time, Uniserve said it aims to establish a 2MW data center in Vancouver to "further service its existing customer base and increase its ability to service a growing AI market."

It then subsequently announced it has entered into a lease with 369 Terminal Holdings Ltd. to develop a data center next door.

Located at 369 Terminal Avenue in Vancouver, the neighboring VAN-2 is set to span approximately 10,000 square feet (929 sqm) and be designed to support enterprise computing, cloud infrastructure, colocation and AI-related workloads. The eight-story multi-tenant office building totals around 160,000 sq ft (14,864 sqm).

The company is targeting an initial operating capacity of 1MW in Q4 2026, with an additional megawatt available for future expansion. The site will be able to support up to 30kW per rack.

Uniserve has also previously announced that BC Hydro has committed to upgrade the facility’s distribution infrastructure to provide up to 3MW of utility power by 2028

Gautam Lohia, Uniserve CEO, said: "VAN-2 represents another important step in building Uniserve's Canadian sovereign digital infrastructure platform. Our focus is on executing a disciplined expansion strategy that combines infrastructure, technical expertise, and integrated services to meet evolving enterprise and AI computing requirements. We believe this approach positions Uniserve to build long-term customer relationships, grow recurring revenue, and create sustainable shareholder value."

Uniserve is now pitching itself as a sovereign Canadian digital infrastructure platform providing managed IT services, cybersecurity, AI services, cloud solutions, and data center infrastructure to customers across Canada.

The company last month announced an enterprise client for AI compute services using two Nvidia B300 GPU-based servers to be deployed at Uniserve's Vancouver data center. The five-year agreement is set to total US$3.15m. Equipment delivery, installation, and service activation are expected to occur before year-end.

stories.title: Infineon and Nvidia to develop gallium nitride power conversion tech for 800VDC data center racks
stories.summary: Latest agreement in support of the move to 800VDC
stories.content:
Infineon has partnered with Nvidia to develop gallium nitride (GaN) power conversion technology for 800 VDC data center architectures.

The German chipmaker announced the tie-up at Nvidia’s GTC Berlin developer conference, building on a May 2025 agreement detailed in October 2025 that focused on serviceable, hot-swappable 800 VDC server racks.

The latest agreement will focus on developing high-voltage intermediate bus converters (IBCs). IBCs step down the main bus voltage feeding accelerator cards to a lower-voltage rail, allowing downstream stages to generate the core and point-of-load rails AI processors need.

Infineon said the multi-stage approach reduces distribution losses while meeting limits on board area, thermals, and uptime. It added that 800 VDC is being introduced alongside existing AC and lower-voltage DC architectures as an additional option for higher-density compute.

Infineon claims GaN switches faster than silicon and with lower losses, enabling switching frequencies up to 1MHz at the IBC stage. The company asserts this lets magnetics and passives shrink, increasing power density and reducing board height. The company said this matters as rack power levels approach the megawatt range.

Infineon's GaN portfolio covers 800V-to-50V, 800V-to-12V, and 800V-to-6V conversion. Infineon pairs the devices with its PSoC Control C3 and EiceDRIVER product families to offer full IBC system solutions. It also offers IBC solutions in silicon and silicon carbide.

“AI is fundamentally reshaping the demands we place on power infrastructure, and semiconductors are at the heart of solving that challenge,” said Jochen Hanebeck, CEO, Infineon Technologies AG. “Our collaboration with Nvidia on 800V power architectures shows what is possible when deep semiconductor expertise meets the pace of innovation required by AI. Gallium nitride-based system solutions are a key enabler of this next generation of data centers, and Infineon is proud to help power the AI era from grid to core.”

The agreement follows a deal with Estonian power and storage systems supplier Skeleton Technologies last month, which will see the companies jointly explore and develop advanced architectures for the entire AI data center power chain, from the grid to the facility itself. This will include Solid State Transformers for medium-voltage AC-to-high-voltage DC conversion.

Infineon is one of Europe's largest semiconductor manufacturers. Spun out of Siemens in 1999, the company specializes in power electronics, automotive microcontrollers, sensors, and security chips. Recently, it increased its research and development in power infrastructure for the data center sector, partnering with Korean electrical equipment manufacturer LS Electric to develop direct current power infrastructure for the AI data center market earlier this year.

stories.title: Data centers face power crunch from AI growth
stories.summary: Data center operators can delay, but not avoid, the need for new electricity infrastructure to support AI computing, an Infosys analysis concludes. Demand-side measures like efficiency gains and flexible workloads can provide usable capacity sooner than grid upgrades.
stories.content:
Data center operators grappling with power constraints can accommodate more AI computing by improving efficiency and shifting flexible workloads, according to a new Infosys analysis. These measures, however, are unlikely to eliminate the need for new electricity infrastructure.The report, which examines AI energy demand through 2030, suggests that demand-side solutions can deliver usable capacity faster than new generation, transmission, and grid upgrades. Mit Majumdar, executive vice president and global head of services, utilities, resources, and energy at Infosys, told Data Center Knowledge that AI-driven energy management, advanced cooling, and peak-load optimisation can create meaningful near-term headroom.Majumdar emphasised a dual-track strategy: maximise existing capacity while accelerating investment in generation, transmission, and grid modernisation. He stated that flexible workloads such as model training and batch processing can be scheduled around grid conditions. Real-time inference and customer-facing applications generally cannot.Broader flexibility will require new commercial models, including workload-aware service-level agreements (SLAs), demand-response incentives, and pricing structures. These measures would reward customers for shifting non-urgent computing.The Infosys analysis also recommends staged construction rather than locking in every project phase based on current assumptions. This modular approach allows capacity to scale as demand evolves and preserves flexibility to benefit from advances in AI models, chips, and cooling technologies. Majumdar said the goal is to avoid both overbuilding and underestimating long-term demand.For utilities, projections of demand-side savings are insufficient for supporting new data center connections. Majumdar advised that utilities should require measurable and verifiable proof of load reductions. This includes historical performance, real-time monitoring, and contractual commitments to reduce load when needed.Risk for promised flexibility should be shared between operators and utilities. Operators should back performance claims with guarantees, while utilities establish clear qualification and verification standards to ensure reliability, Majumdar added.

stories.title: Flexible grid access cuts AI data center power wait times
stories.summary: AI data centers can reduce electricity connection waiting times from 5-10 years to 2-4 years by accepting flexible grid connections. This approach, outlined in a Boston Consulting Group (BCG) report, involves using on-site power generation and storage.
stories.content:
Data centers supporting artificial intelligence (AI) could reduce their electricity connection waiting time from 5-10 years to 2-4 years, according to a report by Boston Consulting Group (BCG). This reduction is achievable by accepting flexible grid connections and using their own power generation and storage systems.“Flexible access can reduce time to power from 5-10+ years to 2-4 years by lowering the need for (major) grid reinforcement,” the report stated. This approach enables data centers to become operational earlier while reducing pressure on electricity grids and limiting additional costs for other power consumers.The analysis focused on five Northwest European markets—the UK, Germany, France, Belgium, and the Netherlands—over the 2030-2035 investment period. BCG noted that power availability has become a major constraint on data center expansion, with connection queues in several markets stretching for years.Global data center power demand is projected to reach around 210 gigawatts by 2030, compared with 84 gigawatts in 2025, according to the report’s estimates. Under the proposed approach, data centers could accept non-firm electricity connections, where power supply may be reduced during periods of grid congestion.They could use on-site generation, batteries, and flexible computing workloads to maintain operations during such periods. Connecting earlier could unlock significant financial benefits, BCG said.For a modelled 150-megawatt AI inference data center in Northwest Europe, connecting three years earlier could generate an estimated $1.28 billion in additional profits before accounting for on-site power asset costs. However, an off-grid setup could increase annual power supply costs by 70-230 per cent compared with a firm grid connection, depending on how power asset costs are accounted for.BCG also suggested that grid-positive data centers could help spread fixed electricity network costs across a larger consumption base. This would reduce the need for additional power generation and grid infrastructure. “Whether a data center burdens or strengthens the system depends on how and where it connects, and how it runs once it is online,” the report concluded.The report called for governments to develop national data center strategies, guide projects towards locations with available grid capacity, and speed up approvals for on-site power assets. It also recommended that grid operators make flexible connections a standard option rather than an exception.

stories.title: US considering 35 data center-related developments on public land, land records say
stories.summary: 17 relate to campuses, 13 to broader AI infrastructure
stories.content:
The US Bureau of Land Management is considering 35 data center-related applications for developments on public land in the western US, according to a tracker published by the Center for Western Priorities.

Of these 35 applications, the tracker, which is based on the Bureau of Land Management’s land records, identified 17 applications to build data center campuses and 13 applications for supporting infrastructure for AI data centers.

The remaining five applications could not be classified into either category based on the information available.

According to the Center for Western Priorities, some of the proposals “dwarf” typical data center constructions, with one cited project in eastern Utah covering more than 9,000 acres and being powered by small modular nuclear reactors.

The Center for Western Priorities’ tracker and map has further details on individual sites.

The organization says it is a non-partisan conservation group, aiming to provide a source of accurate information and promote responsible policies, practices, and accountability in the American West.

In a statement accompanying the release of the tracker, the group said the Trump administration should be forced to solicit feedback on putting data centers on public land.

“Data centers are not like oil, gas, or minerals, which are extracted from public lands because that’s where they exist,” said Lauren Bogard, deputy director of the Center for Western Priorities. “Unlike mining or drilling, there are no natural resources that make it necessary to develop data centers on public lands, and there is no reason to assume data centers belong on them.

“Before even considering putting data centers on public lands, the Trump administration should be obligated to solicit public feedback on this idea. None of these projects should move forward without a permitting framework that lets communities decide where, how, or if data centers get built. That process must include robust, site-specific environmental review and public input opportunities, as well as meaningful, negotiated community benefits that ensure the public is compensated when private companies profit from public lands.”

## Public benefits for public consent

Data center development is increasingly becoming an issue of public consent.

Earlier this week, the US Chamber of Commerce released a report detailing the economic impacts of data centers on local areas.

The organization claimed that data centers are “economic engines powering America’s future” and deliver sustained economic growth for decades.

According to the report, during a typical two-year construction phase, a single data center development can support an average of 5,200 jobs in a state, add $680 million to the state economy, and generate $400 million in state personal income annually.

Citing several major developments across four major counties, Dallas County, Texas; Prince William County, Virginia; Fulton County, Georgia; and Franklin County, Ohio, the report said the average five-year impact on tax revenue can range from $96 million to $174m.

A typical 50MW data center could provide 750 additional workers to the workforce, 740 permanent jobs per year statewide, and generate $125m in tax income annually.

Despite the purported benefits, there remain significant concerns about the impact of data centers on local communities. The issue continues to be a hot topic in the US government, especially as mid-term elections approach.

Just yesterday, US President Donald Trump suggested data center developers should pay a “dividend” to local communities in order to assuage concerns.

Building on decades of experience in mission critical cooling, STULZ has established itself as a recognized industry leader in the design, development, and application of precision climate control technologies for data centers and other critical environments. Whether you’re building liquid cooled data centers or integrating Liquid Cooling into existing aircooled infrastructure, we’re ready to provide the answers and guidance,” said- Valeria Mercante, Liquid Cooling Solutions, Global Product Management.

STULZ has established production sites in China, Germany, India, Italy, and Spain supporting its Asia Hub operations, while STULZ Test Centers ensure reliability by validating every unit under real-world and extreme conditions.

#### **From air to liquid** 

Most existing data center facilities are designed for traditional workloads that utilize air to cool IT equipment. However with the introduction of artificial intelligence (AI) and high performance computing (HPC), Data centre operators are increasingly seeking guidance to make the transformation to liquid cooling or hybrid cooling infrastructure.

For this reason, infrastructure changes must be carefully engineered, rigorously validated, and implemented through controlled, phased deployment strategies. #### **From chip to chiller**

### **Data center buildouts have become complex projects from the proposal to buildout. One slipped deadline risks bringing the entire project to a halt but an experienced partner can manage that complexity with ease.**

The unending appetite for AI has brought about a change within the very facilities that power the technology. Where data centers have generally been CPU-centric, AI data centers rely on power-guzzling GPUs which are pushing rack power draws to 100 kW and beyond, with facilities now pulling anywhere from 100 MW to 1 GW.

Demand for AI computing isn’t slowing down, with estimates suggesting that the value of the AI market is set to increase 25-fold by 2033. That demand is hamstrung by complexity. Securing land and power can take upwards of three years leading to paper-thin margins for buildout timelines.

With margins so thin, a single logistics delay, a mismatched component, or a construction team that isn’t properly staffed can bring an entire buildout to a screeching halt, jeopardizing even the most well considered plans.

#### **Density is only the beginning**

Stalwarts of the sector will remember when a data center was no more than a few server racks in an air-conditioned room. Today AI facilities span hundreds of acres and require cooling technology older facilities can’t support, higher voltage and amperage than before, and networking that can’t lag by so much as a millisecond.

In some parts of the world, energy density within AI data centers has more than tripled compared to traditional data centers. This not only adds complexity to the power procurement process, it changes the pre-development conversation for the facility itself.

This density creates other considerations that must be made including how power is delivered throughout the facility and how backup power will factor into the operations. Each of these thousands of components must be sourced and scheduled to arrive as it is needed.

#### **Where buildouts actually break**

As with any chain, one weak link in a supply chain can bring a project to its knees.

By partnering with Wesco Anixter, you are bringing a trusted partner onboard that has a global network of integrators, contractors and installers. Through this network, every aspect of a buildout is accounted for from design to orchestration to project management. Not only is Wesco Anixter managing the project’s supply chain, it’s accounting for every eventuality.

With margins being so thin, a project can be delayed for months because of one missed delivery. This delay cascades down the chain and suddenly the construction teams and technicians who were only meant to be on site for a week are there for another two. With Wesco Anixter coming in early, it is able to effectively manage these risks because it identifies every aspect of a buildout and coordinates it from procurement to installation.

Whether it’s geopolitical upsets or a new project in unfamiliar territory, the location can make managing a buildout just that much more complicated. This problem becomes exponentially worse as buildouts lean on more vendors from around the world, especially if the site of the project is located in a country that restricts imports from the country a vendor is located in. With its global reach, Wesco Anixter is able to effectively navigate these pitfalls before they even become a problem.

This complexity is manageable, but managing it effectively demands a partner that coordinates the work across the entire timeline. From planning and specification through procurement and execution. If a trusted partner is brought on as soon as possible, problems can be headed off at the pass.

#### **Fewer hand offs, fewer delays**

Coordinating complex projects and managing them is what Wesco Anixter excels in. The company’s experience in the sector means it isn’t just a partner, but a single point of coordination across the entire buildout from beginning to end and even long after.

Gaps between design and construction are managed through end-to-end coordination and visibility across all partners and phases. stories.title: Could market volatility affect DayOne’s IPO?
stories.summary: DayOne Data Centers (DayOne), a Singapore based data center operator, is reportedly considering delaying its planned US initial public offering (IPO) or reducing the size of the share sale amid growing volatility in the data center sector. The company was previously considering raising US$ 5 billion through the IPO, potentially in the fourth quarter, with […]
stories.content:
DayOne Data Centers (DayOne), a Singapore based data center operator, is reportedly considering delaying its planned US initial public offering (IPO) or reducing the size of the share sale amid growing volatility in the data center sector. The company was previously considering raising US$ 5 billion through the IPO, potentially in the fourth quarter, with a targeted valuation of approximately US$ 20 billion.

According to a report from Bloomberg, the company has been assessing market conditions while waiting for an opportune window to launch the listing. One option under consideration is to postpone the IPO until market sentiment improves.

Alternatively, DayOne could proceed with a smaller offering targeting between US$ 2.5 billion and US$ 3 billion, approximately half its original fundraising target. Backed by investors including Coatue and Hillhouse, DayOne continues to engage with prospective investors and remains keen to proceed with the listing as soon as market conditions permit, the people said.

DayOne had filed a Form F-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for its proposed IPO of ADSs on Nasdaq under the ticker “DODC” in early October. Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan, BofA Securities and Citigroup were appointed as underwriters, while the offering size and price range had yet to be determined.

So far, Day One itself has not made any official statement about any postponement. Discussions are still ongoing and DayOne could still proceed with the offering in the coming weeks, depending on market conditions. The latest considerations highlight the challenges facing data center operators seeking to tap public markets amid heightened volatility and shifting investor sentiment towards the sector.
